title: Apply an Integrated Responsible AI Framework to Sustain the Assessment of Learning Effectiveness
summary: Assembles a responsible-AI workflow for judging teaching effectiveness from student data, combining an interpretable decision tree as the global model, SHAP-style explanation, and an adversarial training stage meant to probe rather than fool the model. Synthetic student records at three and five times the size of the real training set are generated and used as the adversarial examples, so the authors can see where the interpretable model's predictive ability breaks down. Two generators produce them, CTGAN and the R package Synthpop, each configured to emit matched volumes and each yielding its own family of adversarially trained models; Synthpop's reach 0.756 accuracy against CTGAN's best of 0.715, though the paper notes CTGAN still supplies the diverse volume needed to probe over- and underfitting. SDV's generator is therefore trained and sampled for one stage of a study whose subject is the explainability framework.
evidence: the method section states that both the CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) and Synthpop (Nowok et al., 2016) methods were applied to generate synthetic data for training the XAI models and searching the optimal models; the experimental section states that the CTGAN model was configured to generate the same amount of training samples as the Synthpop model for training with the decision tree model, denoted ATM-3 and ATM-4; the results state that although CTGAN used three different amounts of synthetic data for ATM-3, ATM-4 and ATM-5 the highest model accuracy was 0.715 while the highest accuracy of Synthpop was 0.756, and that the CTGAN-based models could still generate a large amount of diverse synthetic data to explore whether the models were overfitting or underfitting; the bibliography carries Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN, NeurIPS 2019

title: HDLSS Raman Spectroscopy Data Generation Using GANs and Genetic Algorithms
summary: Works in the high-dimension low-sample-size regime of surface-enhanced resonance Raman spectroscopy, where a clinical serum study yields only 37 patients but each spectrum is long, and asks whether a genetic algorithm can tune a generator well enough to synthesise usable spectra for acute myocardial infarction detection. A basic genetic algorithm and NSGA-II search the hyperparameter space of three architectures, with a weighted sum of cosine similarity, likeness score, Wasserstein distance and Euclidean distance as the fitness function, and the search-optimised models beat manually tuned ones. CTGAN is one of the three architectures trained and searched, alongside WGAN-GP and CTAB-GAN+, and its own hyperparameters are the search space, with the paper referring readers to Xu et al. for their definitions. The paper reports CTGAN as the architecture that collapses at these sample sizes, being the most sensitive to the minimum sample number, so an SDV generator is run as a full arm of a study whose entire empirical program is generator behaviour.
evidence: the abstract states that the study explores variants of genetic algorithms, a basic GA and NSGA-II, to optimise hyperparameters for three GANs, WGAN-GP, CTGAN and CTAB-GAN+, aimed at generating synthetic SERRS data; the methods state that the authors test the effectiveness of Basic GA and NSGA-II on optimising the hyperparameters of three GAN architectures, namely WGAN-GP, CTGAN and CTAB-GAN+, on a dataset of 37 patients; the hyperparameter table gives upper and lower bounds for CTGAN's epochs, batch, discriminator layer 1 and 2 and generator layer, referring the reader to the original papers (Gulrajani et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2022) for a definition of each hyperparameter; the discussion states that NSGA-II performs marginally better on GANs that do not collapse, naming WGAN-GP and CTAB-GAN+, and attributes CTGAN's sensitivity to the minimum sample number to its conditional distribution handling

title: Development and Validation of a Machine Learning Approach for Automated Severity Assessment of COVID-19 Based on Clinical and Imaging Data: Retrospective Study
summary: Builds and validates models that flag severe or critical COVID-19 from routine clinical variables and CT-derived features across two Chinese hospitals, reporting AUC and F1 alongside SHAP attributions so clinicians can see which inputs drive a prediction. Severe cases are rare in the cohort, an imbalance ratio of 0.07, so the study tests four oversampling treatments to raise the minority share to 0.3 and measures the change each produces: SMOTE, adaptive synthetic sampling, geometric SMOTE, and CTGAN. For the CTGAN arm the model is fitted on the training set and sampled to top up the minority class, with results reported on the untouched test set, and oversampling is found to help F1 more than AUC. SDV's generator is thus run as one of four interchangeable treatments inside a study about clinical severity prediction.

title: Utility Metrics for Evaluating Synthetic Health Data Generation Methods: Validation Study
summary: Tests whether the utility metrics people report for synthetic health data can actually rank competing generators the way a downstream modeller would, by generating synthetic versions of 30 heterogeneous health datasets, fitting logistic regression prediction models on real and synthetic data, and checking which metric orders the generators consistently with the observed AUROC and AUPRC gaps. A multivariate Hellinger distance computed over a Gaussian copula representation of the real and synthetic joint distributions comes out best, and an aggregate of several metrics adds almost nothing over it. Three generative models supply the variation the metrics are ranked against, and the first of them is the conditional GAN of Xu et al., the other two being a differentially private Bayesian network and sequential synthesis with decision trees. SDV's generator is therefore run across all 30 datasets as one of three arms in a study whose subject is the metrics rather than the generators.

title: Improved Techniques for Training Tabular GANs Using Cramer's V Statistics
summary: Starts from a known weakness of CTGAN, that it does not preserve dependencies between categorical columns, and asks whether making that dependency structure explicit during training fixes it. Cramer's V, the natural correlation measure for pairs of categorical variables, is introduced into training two ways: as a penalty term added to the generator's loss, and by extending the critic's input with a Cramer's V matrix computed per batch so it can detect categorical dependencies directly. On three benchmark datasets the modified model raises the averaged accuracy of supervised models trained on its output by 11 percent over the unmodified CTGAN, and the paper reports the effect on integrity and contingency similarity. The modification is made inside CTGAN's own loss and critic rather than around a frozen model, and CTGAN is both the substrate and the comparison, so this is a derivative of CTGAN even though the resulting model is never given a name of its own.

title: Mining Production Behavior Without Mining Customer Data: An AI Approach to Test Generation in Regulated Environments
summary: Sketches a five-stage architecture for teams who need realistic test suites for production systems but cannot touch customer records, chaining a privacy filtering layer, a synthetic behaviour generator over event logs, search-based whole-suite test generation driven by branch coverage and mutation score, and federated learning across institutions. It is a conceptual synthesis rather than an implementation: the results section is a comparison table of privacy mechanisms assembled from the cited literature, and no generator is trained or evaluated anywhere in the paper. CTGAN supplies the design of the generation stage, which adopts mode-specific normalization and conditional generation for the mixed continuous and categorical fields of production logs on the basis of Xu et al.; a review table also records CTGAN with a reported utility retention of about 91 percent. This is the adopted-but-not-run pattern: CTGAN's mechanisms are specified as the architecture without any SDV code being executed.
evidence: the literature review states that to overcome mode collapse and imbalance in columns that are a mix of continuous and categorical data like transactional and production logs, Xu et al. proposed conditional tabular GAN (CTGAN), reference 11, by normalizing the data in a mode-specific way and using a conditional generator; section 3.3, Synthetic Behaviour Generation, states that because production logs generally have mixed continuous and categorical fields, mode-specific normalisation and conditional generation are used to avoid mode collapse in imbalanced categorical fields, based on the conditional tabular GAN design, reference 11; the table of synthetic data generation studies lists Xu et al., mixed-type tabular data, Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), utility retention approximately 91 percent; section 4 is a comparison of properties synthesized from the cited literature and the paper reports no experiment of its own
